profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the reference-architecture lead and the MLOps integration lead in the Teaming.AI consortium, held three working days before the automotive pilot team receives the next integration bundle. The architecture workstream has packaged the knowledge-graph layer, scene-analysis event contracts, and runtime ethical-policy checks; the MLOps workstream is connecting those assets into the experimentation and deployment path for relational ML models that will generate operator-facing recommendations on the pilot line. The agenda is to confirm what will be included in the upcoming pilot milestone package, which exact graph artifact the pilot training run will use, what 'monitoring' the automotive partner should see in the shared handoff environment, and how incoming pilot-side integration issues will be handled once the package is with the external team. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear handoff plan, a shared sense that the milestone is on track, and an implicit division of responsibilities across the two workstreams.

members.name: Elena Varga
members.expertise: Distributed systems, semantic integration, industrial knowledge graphs, event-driven software architecture
members.background: Elena leads the cross-partner architecture work package for Teaming.AI and previously built industrial IoT and manufacturing data platforms used across multiple plants. She is responsible for keeping the reference software architecture coherent across pilots, especially where shared interfaces, ontology versions, and observability contracts need to remain stable enough for external adopters.
members.private_state: She wants the automotive milestone to look controlled and reusable ahead of the next consortium review, and she is trying to prevent pilot-specific shortcuts from quietly becoming de facto architecture commitments or creating support chaos once the external team starts integrating.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the package is 'pilot-ready,' they mean the milestone package is safe for an external pilot team to integrate against as a stable reference point, even if internal implementation details still evolve afterward.

The 'current graph snapshot' in cross-workstream coordination refers to the nightly RDF export in the shared object store, because that is the governed artifact aligned with the published ontology version and therefore the only one she considers handoff-grade.
In this project, 'monitoring' naturally includes the human-AI teaming and ethics outputs the architecture was designed to expose at runtime, not just service-operability signals.

Once the pilot begins integrating, pilot-raised issues that touch shared interfaces should be triaged through architecture first so the response stays consistent with the reference architecture and does not fragment across workstreams.

members.name: Jonas Richter
members.expertise: ML pipelines, deployment automation, experiment tracking, operationalization of industrial AI systems
members.background: Jonas coordinates how research models and data-processing components move from experimentation into pilot deployments. He came from an applied ML engineering group, works closely with data scientists and pilot IT contacts, and is used to keeping integrations moving by favoring runnable paths over process-heavy stabilization steps.
members.private_state: He wants the automotive pilot to receive something they can execute and iterate on immediately, and he is wary that architecture-level gatekeeping will slow fixes or force the pilot to wait for formally packaged artifacts that lag behind the latest working pipeline state.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the package is 'pilot-ready,' they mean the pilot can run an end-to-end flow in the shared environment at the milestone date, even if some contracts or payload details get refined in the following sprint.

The 'current graph snapshot' means the latest materialized property-graph dataset already consumed by the feature and training pipeline, because that is the artifact that reflects the most recent enrichment and is operationally current from his team's perspective.

For a handoff like this, 'monitoring' mainly means the signals needed to tell whether jobs, model serving, and connectors are functioning in the pilot environment; teaming and ethical-policy views are separate unless the pilot explicitly asks for them.

Once the pilot starts sending integration issues, the team implementing the affected connector or pipeline should answer directly and quickly; architecture only needs to be involved if a problem later turns out to require a contract change.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the pilot milestone being 'pilot-ready'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the milestone package needs to be 'pilot-ready' by next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 hears 'pilot-ready' as a milestone label meaning the automotive partner can begin integration against a sufficiently stable, versioned package without expecting near-term breaking changes to interfaces or schemas.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 hears 'pilot-ready' as a milestone label meaning the automotive partner can execute a full demonstration path next week, even if fields, schemas, or integration details are still adjusted as the flow is hardened.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because 'pilot-ready' is treated as familiar project shorthand for a milestone rather than as a technical acceptance criterion, both speakers hear ordinary alignment on schedule and readiness while silently applying different standards for what qualifies.

misalignment_points.topic: Which graph artifact counts as the 'current graph snapshot'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using the 'current graph snapshot' for the automotive pilot training run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the nightly RDF export in the shared object store, aligned with ontology v0.9.3 and intended as the governed baseline artifact for cross-partner exchange.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the latest materialized property-graph dump produced after the most recent label-enrichment step in the feature pipeline, which contains derived relations already used by his training jobs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the project, both artifacts are routinely called 'the graph snapshot,' and each is genuinely current within its own workflow, so neither participant has reason to suspect the other is mentally pointing to a different concrete file and representation.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of 'monitoring' in the handoff environment
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that 'monitoring' should be available to the pilot team in the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes monitoring covers the broader runtime outputs central to the reference architecture: human-AI teaming indicators, ethical-policy validation events, scene-analysis alerts, and system observability, ideally exposed through one pilot-facing feed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes monitoring covers the operational signals needed to keep the ML and integration path running: pipeline/job status, inference latency, connector failures, model version, and related health checks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Monitoring is an overloaded but perfectly ordinary engineering term, and the narrower operational subset sounds compatible with the broader architecture-level meaning, so surface agreement feels natural instead of suspicious.

misalignment_points.topic: Who owns pilot-raised integration issues after handoff
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that pilot integration issues should be 'picked up quickly' once the package is with the automotive team.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes incoming pilot-side issues first come through the architecture team for triage, especially when they involve shared contracts, so architecture can route them and prevent ad hoc fixes from quietly changing the reference interfaces.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes pilot-side issues should go directly to whichever implementation team owns the failing connector, training job, or deployment component, with architecture consulted only if a deeper contract question emerges.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both want fast response and use the same language about quick pickup, but the hidden difference is in the path an issue should take before work starts; that workflow assumption feels too obvious and situational to either participant to spell out.
